For James Richardson Gerard, juke-step Jerry, little wrestler, soul-mess of sinew and mind-sight, fired spark, joyed Jesuit, grief-clog too, but a Pan-flute in every Ave, you half-nelson the syntax dandies, ram them to canvas, sit upon and pin the god-fops, minions of ghost tomes, trite chimes, though you walk among them, too, jig and roar of black-robed stroll in golden-grove and choral iambs. You were, yes, that falcon flight, the labor, soar, and dive, but buzzard nose for carrion, too, sniffed your own, knew, alone, the rot, rope-knot or buckle of roots under-on rock, your gowned back to roses, rosaries, but eyes a song gone up, too, sickly little wings stuck in God-glue air: how long? You sang one dialectic flight, sir—the only kind. How high can the swallow swoop, how low the falcon grieve, relieve, in fall till pinions hold him, there, to kill? Light- weight, mutt, heaver of iron, scrap,feather: I believe the hurt, believe you saw what you saw.

Because the original text is a deeply poetic, stream-of-consciousness literary tribute (heavily inspired by the style of poet Gerard Manley Hopkins), "polishing" it requires a delicate touch. A traditional corporate or academic "professional" edit would destroy its artistic voice. 

Below are three ways to refine the text, depending on the level of polish you desire.

### Option 1: Elevated & Lyrical Prose (Recommended)
*This version preserves all of your original striking imagery, compound words, and raw emotion, but smooths the syntax and punctuation to make it flow with high-literary eloquence.*

> For James Richardson Gerard—“juke-step Jerry,” the little wrestler, a soul-mess of sinew and mind-sight, a fired spark, a joyful Jesuit, yet clogged with grief, piping a Pan-flute in every *Ave*. You put the syntax dandies in a half-nelson, ramming them to the canvas to pin those god-fops, those minions of ghost-tomes and trite chimes. 
> 
> Though you walked among them—a black-robed stroll jigging and roaring through golden groves and choral iambs—you were that falcon’s flight: the labor, the soar, the dive. Yet you bore a buzzard’s nose for carrion, too. You sniffed out your own mortality, knowing alone the rot, the rope-knot, and the buckle of roots over rock. With your gowned back turned to roses and rosaries, your eyes remained a song lifted upward, even as sickly little wings felt stuck in the God-glued air: *how long?* 
> 
> You sang a single dialectic flight, sir—the only kind that matters. How high can the swallow swoop? How low can the falcon grieve, relieving its fall only when pinions catch the wind to strike? Lightweight, mutt, heaver of iron, scrap, and feather: I believe your hurt. I believe you saw what you saw.

---

### Option 2: Structured & Refined Tribute
*This version translates the stream-of-consciousness style into a slightly more formal, polished literary essay while retaining every detail and metaphor.*

> This is for James Richardson Gerard: “juke-step Jerry,” the fierce little wrestler, a complex dynamic of sinew, vision, and spirit. A blazing spark and a joyful Jesuit, you were burdened by grief, yet you managed to sound a Pan-flute in every *Ave*. You wrestled the pretenders of syntax into submission, pinning those vain pedants and devotees of hollow, trite prose. 
> 
> Even as you walked among them—a black-robed presence strolling through golden groves to the rhythm of choral iambs—you embodied the flight of a falcon: laboring, soaring, and diving. Yet, with a scavenger's instinct, you also faced life's darker realities. You recognized your own decay, standing alone before the knot of the rope and the buckle of roots against stone. Though your back was turned to conventional roses and rosaries, your gaze was ever fixed upward—a fragile song striving against an oppressive, god-heavy air: *how long?* 
> 
> Yours was a dialectic flight of extremes—the only true kind. How high can the swallow swoop, and how low can the grieving falcon fall before its wings hold firm to strike? Lightweight, underdog, heaver of iron, scrap, and feather: I believe in your pain, and I believe you truly saw what you saw.

---

### Key Adjustments Made:
* **Syntax & Rhythm:** Fixed run-on structures and chaotic comma splices to improve readability without sacrificing the rhythmic, energetic cadence.
* **Clarity of Metaphors:** Clarified complex phrasing like "under-on rock" and "God-glue air" while retaining the exact original imagery.
* **Punctuation:** Used em-dashes, italics, and proper capitalization to guide the reader through the dense, poetic phrasing smoothly.

Here is a expanded, cohesive essay based on the provided points:

***

At the heart of the subject’s life and work lies a profound and complex duality. Far from portraying a static or tranquil piety, he embodies a dynamic, volatile tension: a fierce, joyful religious devotion intertwined with an almost aggressive physical subversion of rigid artistic and intellectual conventions. He does not merely inhabit traditional forms; he ruptures them through a visceral, body-centered engagement with language and belief. By grounding the divine in the raw realities of human experience, he transforms quiet, conventional faith into a site of radical aesthetic and spiritual disruption.

This subversive energy, however, was not born of detached rebellion, but of intense internal friction. Even while fully embedded in the solemnity of sacred rituals and the disciplined constraints of classic poetic forms, the subject endured profound grief and spiritual anxiety. The rigid structures of liturgy and verse served less as a peaceful refuge and more as a crucible. Within these sanctuary spaces, his private anguish vibrated with distinct clarity, demonstrating that formal devotion does not insulate the soul from torment, but can instead sharpen one's awareness of spiritual exile.

Indeed, his entire existence reflects a relentless dialectic between the transcendent and the temporal. He lived perpetually caught between the soaring, ecstatic heights of divine inspiration and the harsh, downward pull of earthly suffering. This vertical tension defines his creative and spiritual output: every upward reach toward sacred illumination is shadowed by the heavy gravity of human limitation. Rather than attempting to smooth over this conflict, his expression embraces the friction, suggesting that genuine revelation is forged precisely at the collision point between divine grace and physical agony.

Compounding this dialectic was a deeply solitary consciousness. Despite his holy calling, the subject possessed an acute, isolated awareness of human mortality, personal decay, and unending internal struggle. He was agonizingly sensitive to the frailty of the flesh and the inexorable passage of time—realities that often left him feeling alienated, even within a community of believers. His sacred vocation did not grant him immunity from existential dread; rather, it heightened his sensitivity to the quiet decay of the self, rendering his internal battles all the more stark and unyielding.

Ultimately, however, this intense suffering is framed not as a failure of faith, but as its essential validation. In the final assessment, the speaker fully honors the subject’s agonizing journey, recognizing that his pain was the crucible through which authentic sight was achieved. By affirming the absolute truth of the subject's spiritual vision, the narrative elevates his earthly torment from mere tragedy to a sacred form of witness. In the end, it is through the very wounds of his mortality and the violent breaking of conventions that his spiritual vision achieves its enduring, unassailable reality.

To read the poetry of James Richardson Gerard is not merely to observe a craftsman at work, but to witness a soul engaged in a desperate, illuminated combat. Gerard’s body of work exists within a crucible where spiritual aspiration and physical agony continuously collide. Rather than offering smooth, comforting meditations on faith or despair, Gerard subjects his medium and himself to a rigorous dialectic. Through intense metaphors of syntactic wrestling and stark imagery that juxtaposes soaring falcon flights with the low rot of carrion, Gerard articulates a profound dual struggle—one simultaneously aesthetic and spiritual—that ultimately yields a terrifying, singular vision of human existence.

At the core of Gerard’s methodology is a violent, deliberate confrontation with the limits of language. For Gerard, verse is not a passive vessel for thought, but a wrestling ring. His poetry frequently employs fractured cadences, abrupt enjambments, and twisted grammatical structures that reflect an internal agony. This "syntactic wrestling" signifies the poet’s struggle to force finite words to hold the infinite weight of divine longing, while remaining pinned under the heavy burden of mortal suffering. Sentences strain against their traditional boundaries; clauses contort and fracture, mirroring a speaker physically and spiritually grappling with an elusive God. In this formal violence, language becomes both the weapon and the wound, capturing the excruciating friction between human limitation and divine desire.

This formal struggle is mirrored in Gerard’s imagery, which operates on a dramatic axis of vertical extremes. On one end of this spectrum is the falcon: a symbol of majestic ascension, razor-sharp perception, and soaring, celestial flight. The falcon represents the soul’s capacity for divine transcendence, breaking free from earthly tethering to navigate the ethereal blinding light of the sacred. Yet, Gerard abruptly yokes this lofty ideal to its absolute opposite: the damp, heavy reality of low carrion rot. In Gerard's lexicon, the flesh is not merely weak; it is subject to decay, stench, and visceral mortality. By forcing the soaring falcon into the same conceptual space as the rotting carcass, Gerard refuses to grant his reader an easy escape into spiritual abstraction. He insists that any contemplation of the divine must account for the maggot-ridden reality of earthly decay.

It is precisely through this dialectical tension—the wrestling of syntax and the clash of height and depth—that Gerard achieves his ultimate artistic breakthrough. He does not resolve his dualities by choosing heaven over earth, or spiritual purity over physical anguish. Instead, Gerard forge a singular, unified vision that encompasses both divine transcendence and deep mortal pain. The light of his spiritual revelation does not erase the shadows of human agony; rather, it illuminates them, revealing that suffering is the very terrain upon which spiritual depth is forged. 

Ultimately, James Richardson Gerard’s work stands as a monumental validation of lived suffering. His poetry proves that true aesthetic and spiritual insight cannot be achieved through comfortable detachment or easy pious platitudes. By bearing witness to the violent beauty of the falcon and the brutal truth of the carrion—and by wrestling that vision into the very syntax of his art—Gerard authenticates the profound sorrow of the human condition, transmuting mortal agony into an enduring, transcendent truth.

Inside the faded leather cover of an old, wooden-bound journal, written in precise, elegant calligraphy, were three simple words: *For James Richardson*. It was a quiet dedication, tucked away from the rest of the world, yet it carried the weight of a lifetime of memory.

James Richardson was a man of few words, but every action he took left a lasting imprint on those around him. As a master craftsman in a small coastal town, his days were measured in the steady rhythm of his work and the care he brought to everything he built. People came from miles away not just for his skill, but for the warmth and patience that filled his workshop. 

The journal had been given to him decades ago by a young apprentice whom James had taken under his wing. Across its yellowed pages were detailed records of every project James had completed, accompanied by notes on the people he had helped along the way. It was a quiet chronicle of a life dedicated to service, craftsmanship, and community.

Years later, the journal remains a cherished keepsake. The inscription on the first page serves as more than just a note of ownership; it stands as a tribute to a mentor, a leader, and a friend. It is a lasting reminder of the gratitude felt by all who knew him, written forever **for James Richardson**.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, rhythmic prose poem in the style of Gerard Manley Hopkins, addressing a priest-poet named James Richardson Gerard who wrestles with language, faith, and physical suffering.
counterfactuals.output: O James, Richardson Gerard! bone-bolted, breath-bound, word-wrestler in the night’s marrow-dark—how you groan under the great, heavy, hover-and-strike of the Spirit! Flesh-fretted, rib-racked, your lung-bellows heave-heavy with the damp draught of the world’s chill, while the ache-iron hammers at the knee-joint, spine-stung, bile-bitter, every nerve a wire strung tight and twitching for the plectrum of torment. How the body betrays, James! How this ash-house, this clay-clod of a frame, buckles beneath the soul’s fierce, sudden, god-glory-surge! Yet you forge—O you forge! You strike at the ink-horn, scratch-scritch on the white leaf-skin, hunting the high, untamed name of Him—the Christ-spark, the world’s freshness, the bright-brimmed flash-and-fire—though the phrase frays, though the tongue stammers in its own spit-silt, tethered, trapped in the poor, pale cage of human speech. You would weld the Word to the Wound! You would syllable the pitch-black agony till it shines like gold-foil, sun-slanted, God-struck! Ah, but He wrestles back, doesn’t He, priest-poet? The Great Smith-God, anvil-heavy on your chest, pressing the air from your lungs till you gasp out your dark-dawn prayer through the tooth-picket: *Lord, Lord, light-leap in this gloom-gully!* And answer comes none but the dry click of the bead-string, the silent, salt-drip of your own brow-sweat, the awful, beautiful, crushing closeness of His absent presence. Still—praise! Praise Him for the rupture, the wrack, the rare-reach of the bruised reed! For even here, in the agony-angle, the body broken to a cross-timber, the word is born—gashed, yes, but grace-gloried, strain-strung, and ringing true! Write, then, James, bleed-scribe, priest of the broken quill! Let the ink-vein burst, let the line leap to shock the silence: for Christ stands footing the ruin of your flesh, bright-blazing through the scar-tissue, catching your wrung-out, beautied, agony-apt song.

counterfactuals.output: O book-broken, grace-grappled Brother Julian, midnight runner through the ink-stained alleys of the mind, we mourn you now, you high-flying, cassock-torn Jesuit of the sacred stacks! How you soared—unhooded, talon-sharp, wind-hovering—into the blinding high-gale of the Logos, an eyas plunging through the incense-smoke of your own burning intellect, only to be dragged back down to the squared-circle of your monastic cell to wrestle the fierce, invisible Angel in an endless midnight agon. You fought God in a full-nelson on the bloody vellum of the desk; sweat of Ignatian exercises dripping off your brow onto the margin-notes; pinned again and again by the heavy, holy weight of truth, yet rising—blood-bright, bone-pounded, sprung-hearted—to snap the earthly jesses of your skull! You were the Lord’s own falconer and His chief heel, taking the suplex of divine revelation right on the chin, hood ripped away, eyes wide to the stark, holy light, until the cosmic referee slammed three final counts upon the floorboards of your heart, freeing your wild, taloned soul to tag out of the mortal ring and dive straight *Ad Maiorem Dei Gloriam* into the dark sky of the Absolute.

*(The speaker stands over the priest, who is kneeling on the cold flagstones of the altar, clutching a rosary as if it were a brass-knuckle dust-up.)*

Look at you, father-fool, crouched in the turnbuckle of your own self-pity, weeping into the canvas! Is it Goldengrove you are grieving for, you soul-sprained jabroni? Are you still whimper-bound because the woods are unleaving? 

Listen to me! Margaret isn’t crying for the blight, and neither should you! It’s *you* on the mat, priest! It is *yourself* you mourn for, caught in a grief-clog of your own making, waiting for some sky-hooked pity that isn’t coming to save you from the count!

You think this faith is a soft thing? You think the Lord Almighty is playing kayfabe with your wretched, rib-cracked spirit? No! He’s the Heavyweight Champion of the Void, and He’s got you locked in a cross-face submission hold of absolute Grace! You want to talk about *The Windhover*? You caught morning’s minion, didn’t you? That dappled-dawn-drawn high-flyer, swooping through the rafters! But what happened when the brute-beauty and the valour crashed down into the squared circle? *Brute-force!* *Rebuff!* It shattered your collarbone, didn’t it? 

You got no-sold by the Holy Ghost!

You sit there in the dark, bleeding out your sweet, delicate iambs, waiting for a savior who doesn't use a script. Well, break the kayfabe, Father! The God-glue that binds your fractured bones to this altar isn't made of holy water—it’s sweat, it’s gristle, it’s the iron-taste of your own pride being suplexed into the dust! 

You preach about the *sheer plod* that makes the plough shine, but you refuse to take the bump! You want the gold title belt of resurrection without taking the stiff shots to the jaw! Look down! Look at the blue-bleak embers of your dying vocation! They don’t just fall, man—they *gall*! They *gash*! They bleed gold-vermilion all over the dirty mat!

So what’s it gonna be? Are you gonna stay down on the floorboards, a sin-slicked, gloom-heavier mess, crying over fallen leaves? Or are you gonna tap out to the Light, pull yourself up by the ropes of your cassock, and cut a promo that shakes the very throne-room of Heaven?

The referee is at eight, priest. *Eight!* Get up, or get pinned by your own damnation!

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an apostrophe to a fictionalized poet named James Richardson Gerard who is part lightweight wrestler, part devout Jesuit, and part bird of prey. Focus on his fight against 'syntax dandies' and his internal struggle with faith and rot.
counterfactuals.output:
O James Richardson Gerard—
one hundred and thirty pounds of bone, feather, and discipline—
you step onto the canvas in a wool cassock,
your knuckles chalked with altar ash and sweat. 
Lightweight, raptor-eyed, servant of the Society:
how your yellow pupils dilate in the gloom of the gym,
searching for the soft, unmuscled throat of the poem.

How you hate them, James! 
Those syntax dandies preening in their gilded salons,
sucking on scented semicolons, 
wearing their enjambments like silk cravats!
You drop from the rafters like a tiercel in a dive-bomb,
hooking talons into their delicate, perfumed iambs.
I see you suplexing their frilly adjectives,
pinning their hollow metaphors to the mat 
until the leather creaks and they choke on their own lace.
*“God is not a lace handkerchief!”* you roar,
driving a elbow into the chest of a bloodless sonnet,
*“God is a heel-hook! God is the strike from the clouds!”*

And yet, Brother Gerard, when the arena clears
and the dandies flee back to their tea rooms,
you are left alone with the incense and the liniment.
You kneel on the wet mat, hollow-boned and shivering,
and the real fight begins—not with men, but with the mold.

You carry the Ignatian fire in a cage of ribs that smells of swamp.
You look into the Host and see the creeping mildew of your own flesh;
you pray the Rosary until your thumbs bleed,
yet you taste only copper, turnip, and decay.
Is it the Jesuit in you that craves the whip,
or the raptor that demands fresh, warm carrion?
You starve yourself to make the weight class of the saints,
purgatorial, sweating out the black bile of doubt,
terrified that Grace is just another term for rot,
that the resurrection is only a thermal lifting a vulture toward a sunless sky.

Fight on, James Richardson Gerard!
Strike at the weak-spined line! Shred the pastel phrase!
Tear the velvet off the verse with a beak forged in Loyola’s dark!
And when the rot creeps up your throat,
when the faith rots in your gullet like an undigested sparrow,
feather your wings, lock the ankle,
and wrestle the angel into the dirt until the dawn breaks, or the bone snaps.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a highly stylized prose piece about a Jesuit who battles both God and grammar.
counterfactuals.output:
The tallow candle guttered, shedding a jaundiced halo upon the vellum. Outside, the night was a silent, unpunctuated void; inside, Father Lucian was committing treason against both Heaven and the humanities.

His weapon was a crow-quill pen; his battleground, a Latin translation of the Gospel of John. But the *Logos* would not bend. The Word was God, the text claimed, but to Lucian, the Word was a slippery, serpentine thing that resisted the iron cage of the nominative case.

“*In principio erat Verbum,*” he muttered, his voice a dry rustle of dry cassock. 

He stared at the page. *Erat*. The imperfect tense. A continuous, lingering past. Was God a state of ongoing, unfinished Being, or a sudden, sharp, definitive perfect? He dipped his nib into the oak-gall ink. To assign a tense to the Eternal was an impiety; to leave it untranslated was an insubordination to his Rector. 

He struck at the parchment, scratching out a copula. The Almighty, he reasoned, refused to be a predicate. God was the ultimate Subject, yet every time Lucian tried to write Him into a sentence, the Lord slipped into the accusative—a passive object, dragged across the syntactical floor by the whims of human verbs.

*You hide behind the passive voice,* Lucian accused, glaring up into the vaulted shadows of his cell. *You bleed into the margins. You demand total obedience, yet You defy the laws of composition!*

Silence met his challenge. God, as usual, answered in the apophatic—the grammar of absence. 

Lucian’s fingers twitched, stained purple-black to the knuckles like a murderer caught in the act of slaughtering syntax. He raged against the comma, that stuttering, indecisive piece of dust. Why must faith tremble in the pause between clauses? He despised the semicolon—that liminal purgatory, too weak to end, too proud to continue. And the subjunctive mood! Ah, the subjunctive was the devil’s own terrain: the realm of *might-be* and *would-that*, the conditional, agonizing space where God remained a probability rather than a noun.

He wanted a Period. He wanted the absolute, heavy, granite thud of a full stop. He wanted God to sit still at the end of a sentence and be defined.

*“I AM THAT I AM,”* the Lord had told Moses. 

“A tautology!” Lucian hissed, striking his knee. “A recursive, arrogant, unparseable loop! Give me a direct object, Lord, or give me a period!”

He began to write frantically, wrestling the divine into submission with a barrage of subordinate clauses. He piled preposition upon preposition—*under* His wrath, *through* His grace, *beyond* His light—trying to build a cage of syntax high enough to reach the throne. He threw dangling modifiers like spears into the dark. He slashed through a split infinitive with the fury of a zealot purging heresy. 

Language broke under his hand. The ink pooled, a black tear spreading across the Holy Text. 

Suddenly, a draft swept through the cell. The candle flame stretched, flared blue, and snapped back.

Lucian froze. The silence changed texture. It grew dense, heavy with an ungrammatical weight. The air smelled of ozone and incense. In the darkness above his desk, a Presence lowered itself—an unnamable, unpunctuated Reality that defied all rules of agreement. It possessed no gender, no case, no declension. It was an Infinite Imperative.

It did not speak in Latin. It did not speak in Greek. It spoke in the terrifying, absolute silence that exists before the first word is ever uttered. 

The quill trembled in Lucian’s hand. He looked down at his manuscript. The ink had blurred the carefully parsed sentences into a single, dark, shapeless stain. 

His eyes watered. His pride collapsed. How could a man measure the ocean with a calliper? How could a mind bound by subject and verb house the screaming, light-shattered vastness of the Uncreated?

Slowly, deliberately, Father Lucian dipped his pen one last time. He did not write a noun. He did not write a verb. He crossed out his sprawling, arrogant, highly structured paragraphs. He erased his theology with a single, sweeping stroke of black.

At the center of the blank, ruined page, beneath the crushing, loving, terrible weight of the Almighty, the Jesuit drew a single, open-ended em-dash—

And held his breath, waiting for God to complete the sentence.
